intuition.text: Nori stands between depot beacons that pull equally in opposite directions. Neither request is weak, but their sum hides both. A sideways probe can change the geometry enough for the beacon group to speak again. That probe breaks the balance; it does not decide which beacon Nori ought to visit.
intuition.situation: Use fallback when Nori’s combined steering is quiet despite competing goals. It is an escape from a local balance, provided moving away is actually desirable.

example.name: Nori between the depot beacons
example.description: Nori starts at rest midway between the West and East beacons, each {beaconHalfSpan} units away along their line. Their seek requests have equal weight {beaconWeight}. The lower group uses engine wander with a fixed direction across that line, towards the bottom of the drawing, and fallback weight {fallbackWeight}. Requests must exceed epsilon {epsilon} units/s²; acceleration is capped at {maxAcceleration} units/s² and speed at {maxSpeed} units/s. Each update takes {timeStep} s. Change the fallback weight or threshold to make the nudge take control or remain silent; the comparison keeps the same threshold and uses weight {weakFallbackWeight}.

steps.title: Measure the combined beacon request
steps.text: Engine seek points at each beacon with full acceleration. Multiply both outputs by beaconWeight, then engine blend sums and clips them. The net request now has magnitude {primaryMagnitude} units/s². At the centre the opposing requests cancel; testing their individual magnitudes would miss that balance.

steps.title: Prepare an independent nudge
steps.text: Engine wander supplies a velocity-matching request from the fixed heading and wander circle. Engine blend applies fallbackWeight and clips the result, currently {fallbackMagnitude} units/s². This separate group contributes nothing while the beacon group has priority, even when its own request is stronger.

steps.title: Fall through only when the net is small
steps.text: Call engine firstActive with the beacon group first and the fallback second. Each must exceed epsilon strictly. The active group is {activeGroup}, supplying magnitude {selectedMagnitude} units/s². If both decline, acceleration is zero. No stalled flag or waiting period is involved.

steps.title: Move, then let the original group try again
steps.text: The local integrator clips the new velocity after acceleration × timeStep, then moves with that velocity. Recompute both groups from the new state. {primaryHandover} {returnReading} Moving away changes the beacon geometry, but a group can reclaim control only if its net request clears the chosen threshold.

visual.textEquivalent: Nori is {lineOffset} units from the line between West and East; {beaconReading}. The sideways fallback requests {fallbackMagnitude} units/s², and {activeGroup} controls this update.

implementations.relevance: gdx-ai provides composable Java steering behaviours. Its blended and priority controllers can place a secondary request after a group whose ingredients might cancel.
implementations.explanation: BlendedSteering accumulates weighted behaviour outputs and limits linear acceleration. PrioritySteering then evaluates behaviours in order, passing on when squared magnitude does not exceed epsilon squared. This makes a cancelling blend eligible to yield to a later behaviour. If all behaviours are small, the controller retains the last result, including a small nonzero one.

references.supports: The book covers equilibrium fallback in Chapter 3 Movement, §3.4.3 Priorities within §3.4 Combining Steering Behaviors.

references.title: gdx-ai 1.8.2 · PrioritySteering.java
references.supports: A small net steering result yields to the next behaviour; the controller returns the first result above its threshold or the last small result.

references.title: gdx-ai 1.8.2 · BlendedSteering.java
references.supports: A blended group adds weighted vectors before limiting the resulting linear acceleration, allowing opposing requests to cancel.

limits: At comparison weight {weakFallbackWeight}, the first request has magnitude {comparisonInitialMagnitude} units/s² against epsilon {epsilon}: {comparisonStart}. Its largest offset is {comparisonMaxOffset} units. A fallback at or below epsilon cannot start Nori from this balance, even though the behaviour is present.
The chosen run reaches an offset of {maxOffset} units and uses fallback for {fallbackSteps} updates. {movementReading} {returnReading} Breaking the balance does not choose a beacon or find a route.

A small net result does not tell us whether Nori is trapped or already content. If both beacon goals are satisfied, the same fallback rule can move Nori away again. A completion condition belongs outside this magnitude test.
Zero acceleration does not stop a moving Nori in this integrator. An already moving body can coast even when both groups decline; only the initially resting case remains still without a request.

nearby.why: Read priority steering for the ordered group test that gives Nori’s fallback its turn.
Read equilibria in blending when diagnosing why the opposing beacon requests cancel before deciding whether a fallback is appropriate.
Use weighted blending to change the beacon group’s balance itself; fallback leaves those conflicting weights intact.
Read wander when the lower group should explore with a changing direction; this probe holds its heading and angle fixed to expose the handover.
Reach for a steering pipeline when Nori needs a target and constraints that resolve the route, rather than another local nudge.
